title: Host Extensions for IP Multicasting
subtitle: How a host sends to, joins, and reports membership in a group of receivers.
summary: RFC 1112 defines what an IP host must do to support multicasting: sending one datagram to a "host group" identified by a class D address (224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255). It adds join and leave operations, a mapping from group addresses to Ethernet multicast addresses, and version 1 of the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP), which tells nearby routers which groups have members. It is Internet Standard STD 5; IGMP itself has since moved to versions 2 and 3.

eli5.summary: Instead of shouting at one person or at everybody, you can send a message to a club, and only the kids who joined the club get it. This RFC says how a computer joins a club, leaves it, and tells the nearby teacher that the club still has members.

questions: how does a host join a multicast group
how are multicast addresses mapped to ethernet
what is a class d address

tldr.problem: IP could send to one host or to everyone on a network, but not to a chosen group of hosts spread across networks.
tldr.mechanism: A group gets a class D address; hosts join it through new IP operations, the local network filters on a mapped multicast address, and IGMP reports tell neighbouring multicast routers which groups have members.
tldr.outcome: This is the base that IP multicast still builds on; later IGMP versions added leave messages and source filtering.

today: IP multicast is still used for service discovery on local networks, IPTV and market data distribution. The host rules in this RFC (class D addresses, the 23-bit Ethernet mapping, joining through the IP layer) are still how hosts work, but the IGMP in its Appendix I is version 1. Current hosts normally run IGMPv2 (RFC 2236) or IGMPv3 (RFC 3376, since revised by RFC 9776), which add explicit leave messages and source filtering. Wireshark and tcpdump decode IGMP, and mainstream operating systems expose group joins to applications through socket options.

implementations.name: Linux, BSD and Windows IP stacks
implementations.note: Implement level 2 host multicast; applications join groups through socket options such as IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IP multicasting is the transmission of an IP datagram to a "host group", a set of zero or more hosts identified by a single IP destination address. Delivery is best-effort, exactly like ordinary unicast IP: the datagram is not guaranteed to arrive at all members or in the same order.

Membership is dynamic. Hosts may join and leave at any time, a host may belong to several groups, and a sender does not have to be a member of the group it sends to. Forwarding between networks is the job of multicast routers; this memo covers only what a host must do, and says the router algorithms will be specified in separate documents.

RFC 1112 obsoletes RFC 988 and RFC 1054, earlier versions of the same specification. It was later updated by RFC 2236.
sections.eli5: Normally you can talk to one friend, or yell so everyone in the room hears. Multicast is like a group chat: you send once, and everybody who joined the chat gets it, even if they live in different houses.

sections.title: Levels of conformance
sections.content:
The RFC does not force every IP implementation to support multicast. It defines three levels. Level 0 hosts have no support and should quietly discard any datagram with a class D destination address that reaches them. Level 1 hosts can send multicast datagrams but cannot receive them or join groups. Level 2 hosts do everything: they can join and leave groups, and they implement IGMP.

Level 1 is deliberately cheap. It lets a host take part in services such as resource location or status reporting with very little new code, and only sections 4, 5 and 6 of the RFC apply to it. Level 2 requires IGMP and extensions to both the IP service interface and the local network service interface.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of kids. Level 0 kids ignore the group chat. Level 1 kids can post in it but can't read it. Level 2 kids can post, read, join and leave.

sections.title: Host group addresses
sections.content:
A group is named by a class D IP address, one whose high-order four bits are 1110. In dotted decimal that is 224.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255. Class E addresses (high bits 1111) are reserved for future addressing modes.

Two addresses are special. 224.0.0.0 is guaranteed never to be assigned to any group. 224.0.0.1 is the permanent group of all IP hosts, including gateways, and addresses every multicast host on the directly connected network. The RFC points out that there is no address for all hosts on the whole Internet, so 224.0.0.1 cannot be used that way.

A group is permanent or transient. For a permanent group it is the address, not the membership, that is permanent: it may have any number of members, even zero. Other addresses are available for transient groups that exist only while they have members. Well-known permanent groups are published in "Assigned Numbers".

A host group address must never appear as the source address, or inside a source route or record route option, of an outgoing datagram. An incoming datagram with a group address as its source is quietly discarded.
sections.eli5: A group chat needs a name. Multicast names are special addresses that start with 224 to 239. The name 224.0.0.1 means "everyone on this street", and it never leaves the street.

sections.title: Sending multicast datagrams
sections.content:
Sending uses the same "Send IP" operation as unicast; the upper-layer protocol simply gives a group address as the destination. The RFC suggests three extensions to the service interface: a way to set the time-to-live (defaulting to 1, so multicasting beyond one network needs an explicit choice), a way to choose the outgoing interface on a multi-homed host, and, for level 2 hosts, a way to inhibit the local copy that is looped back by default when the sender is itself a member.

Inside the IP module, the routing test changes from "destination is on the same local network" to "destination is on the same local network or is a host group", so group traffic goes straight onto the local network instead of to a gateway. Multicast routers attached to that network take over forwarding when the TTL allows.

On Ethernet, the group address is mapped by copying the low-order 23 bits of the IP address into the low-order 23 bits of the Ethernet multicast address 01-00-5E-00-00-00. Because a group address has 28 significant bits, more than one group can map to the same Ethernet address, which is why the IP layer filters again.
sections.eli5: To send to the club you just write the club's name on the envelope. Your computer drops it onto the local wire, and a helper called a multicast router carries it on to other streets if you allowed it to travel that far.

sections.title: Receiving multicast datagrams
sections.content:
To receive, a host must first join. The IP service interface gains two non-blocking operations, JoinHostGroup(group-address, interface) and LeaveHostGroup(group-address, interface). The IP module keeps a list of memberships per interface, with a reference count so several upper-layer protocols can share one membership; the local network module is told only on the first join and last leave.

The local network service interface gets a matching pair, JoinLocalGroup and LeaveLocalGroup, so the network module can update its hardware receive filter. A module may ignore leave requests or deliver extra packets if it cannot filter well, so the IP module drops datagrams for groups it did not join, without any error report or log entry.

Three receive rules are easy to miss: an incoming datagram with TTL 1 is not rejected; an ICMP error is never generated for a datagram sent to a group; and every level 2 host must join 224.0.0.1 on each interface at start-up and stay a member while it is active.
sections.eli5: To hear the club you must raise your hand to say "I'm in". Your computer tells its network card which names to listen for, and throws away any other mail without making a fuss.

sections.title: IGMP message format
sections.content:
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is how hosts report memberships to immediately-neighbouring multicast routers. Like ICMP it is part of IP: messages ride in IP datagrams with protocol number 2. This memo specifies version 1, and says version 0 from RFC 988 is obsolete.

Every message is 8 octets: a 4-bit version (1), a 4-bit type, an 8-bit unused field (zero when sent, ignored when received), a 16-bit checksum, and a 32-bit group address. The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the 8-octet message, computed with the checksum field zeroed. There are two types: 1 is a Host Membership Query and 2 is a Host Membership Report. In a Query the group address is zero; in a Report it carries the group being reported.
sections.eli5: The note a computer passes to the teacher is tiny, just eight bytes. It says whether it is a question or an answer, and, if it is an answer, which club.

sections.title: IGMP operation and state machine
sections.content:
Multicast routers periodically send Queries to 224.0.0.1 with TTL 1. A host answers by sending a Report for each group it belongs to on that interface. To avoid an "implosion" of simultaneous Reports, the host starts a separate timer for each group, set to a random value between zero and D seconds, where D is 10 seconds. When a timer fires, the host sends a Report whose IP destination is the group address itself, with TTL 1.

Because the Report goes to the group, other members on the same network overhear it. A host that hears a Report for a group it belongs to stops its own timer, so normally only one Report is sent per group per network. Routers need to know only that at least one member exists, not who. Queries are normally sent no more than once a minute, and a host that has just joined a group should send a Report at once (and repeat it once or twice) instead of waiting for a Query.

Per group and interface a host is in one of three states: Non-Member, Delaying Member (timer running) or Idle Member (no timer). Membership in 224.0.0.1 is a special case: it starts as Idle Member and is never reported.

IGMPv1 has no leave message. A host leaving a group just stops its timer; a router concludes the group is empty only when Reports for it stop arriving after some number of Queries.
sections.eli5: The teacher asks "who is in which club?" Everyone waits a random moment before answering. If you hear a friend already say "the chess club is here", you stay quiet, because one answer is enough.

sections.title: Group address issues and security
sections.content:
Appendix II is background, not part of the specification. It stresses that a group address is not bound to a set of unicast addresses: routers do not keep a list of members, only the fact that some network has at least one. On Ethernet, a router needs just one multicast address per group that has local members.

The memo does not say how transient group addresses are allocated, and floats ideas such as servers that hand out addresses, algorithmic mapping from higher-level group identifiers (it names VMTP, RFC 1045), or a range for random allocation that tolerates collisions.

The security advice is short and blunt. A host cannot assume that datagrams sent to a group reach only the intended hosts, or that datagrams it receives as a member are meant for it. Misdelivery must be detected above IP, using higher-level identifiers or authentication tokens, and sensitive data should be encrypted or governed by administrative routing controls.
sections.eli5: Anyone can join a club if they know its name, so don't tell secrets to a club. Lock your message in a box that only the right kids can open.

items.title: Level 0
items.text: No multicast support. Quietly discards stray class D datagrams.

items.title: Level 1
items.text: Can send to groups but cannot receive or join. Needs only sections 4 to 6.

items.title: Level 2
items.text: Full support: send, join, leave, and run IGMP.

items.title: Routers are separate
items.text: Multicast routers and their algorithms are out of scope; this RFC covers hosts only.

data.title: Group address to Ethernet multicast address
data.code:
Ethernet base address : 01-00-5E-00-00-00
IP low-order 23 bits  : copied into the low 23 bits

224.1.2.3     -> 01-00-5E-01-02-03
239.1.2.3     -> 01-00-5E-01-02-03   (same Ethernet address)
224.129.2.3   -> 01-00-5E-01-02-03   (same again)

28 significant bits in a group address, 23 copied,
so 32 groups can share one Ethernet address.
